summary:
Abandoned but not Forgotten is an interactive documentary that runs in the browser. You fly to Mars or the Moon, land a short walk from a real machine left there, cross terrain built from NASA elevation data, see the last thing it sent to Earth, and choose to remember it.

Eleven real craft are staged, from Surveyor 3 and Apollo 11's Eagle descent stage to Opportunity, Spirit and Ingenuity. There is no narrator: each story is told by the craft's own last images and data and by real NASA mission audio. A map marks 78 catalogued pieces of hardware left on both worlds, each with its protection status.

The places, the machines and every number are NASA data: HiRISE and LROC elevation models for seven landing sites, JPL orbital elements for today's distance and signal delay, the measured opacity of the 2018 dust storm after which Opportunity fell silent. At Apollo and Surveyor sites the lander sets down over 2 km away, as NASA's heritage recommendations ask. The fiction, a ship and a wormhole, is labelled on screen.

The challenge asks for stories about equipment left behind. We made each machine a place anyone can visit, so that it is remembered.
details:
What it does

Abandoned but not Forgotten is an interactive documentary that runs in the browser, about the machines humanity left on Mars and the Moon. The viewer sits in the cockpit of a fictional exploration ship, crosses a wormhole, lands near a real spacecraft and walks to it in first person. Each visit has five steps: arrival, approach, encounter, last signal, remembering.

Eleven real craft are fully staged. On Mars: Opportunity, Spirit, Ingenuity, InSight, Curiosity, Perseverance and Sojourner. On the Moon: the Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage, the Apollo 17 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Surveyor 3 and Lunokhod 1. Nine can be remembered; Curiosity and Perseverance are still operating, so they are visited but not remembered. An archive shows each craft in one real frame, the last image it sent or one that shows it. A closing sequence re-enacts Artemis II passing behind the Moon on 6 April 2026.

How it works

- Terrain: seven landing sites are built from stereo elevation models, HiRISE (1 m per pixel) on Mars and LROC NAC (2 to 5 m per pixel) on the Moon. Horizons out to 25 km come from HRSC-MOLA and LOLA. Ground colours are measured from real surface photographs of each site.

- Numbers: today's Earth to Mars distance and signal delay are computed from JPL's Keplerian elements by solving Kepler's equation for the current date. The Mars sol counter uses the NASA GISS Mars24 algorithm. Distances are shown to three significant figures.

- The 2018 dust storm: the sky over Opportunity darkens with the opacity the rover measured (tau 0.5 to 10.8). Direct sunlight follows Beer-Lambert attenuation.

- Artemis II: Orion's path comes from NASA/JPL Horizons and was checked against NASA's published closest approach and loss of signal.

- Heritage: at Apollo and Surveyor sites the lander sets down 2.1 to 2.5 km away, following NASA's 2011 recommendations for protecting lunar artifacts.

- Sound: real NASA recordings with subtitles (Apollo mission audio, Perseverance's SuperCam microphone, InSight's seismometer played as sound).

- Every item on screen carries a credit and a source. Pressing I shows where each number comes from.

What is real and what is not

The ship and the wormhole are fiction, and the application says so on screen. Representative elements are labelled ("Representative terrain", "Representative model", "Re-enactment"). No usable elevation model exists for Sojourner's site, so its ground is procedural and labelled as such. Rocks are real photogrammetry scans, but not from those places. What could not be verified was left out or marked.

Benefits and intended impact

These sites are heritage that almost no one will ever visit. The project lets anyone with a browser stand beside them, learn what each machine discovered and how it fell silent, and see how NASA asks future missions to protect them. It works in English and Turkish.

How it is creative

There is no narrator and no score to chase. The story is told by the machines' own last data: the experience opens with the incomplete final image Opportunity sent. The interface is drawn on the inside of a helmet visor: a compass, the signal delay, the days of silence. Remembering is the only goal.

Tools

JavaScript (plain ES modules, no build step), three.js r187 with custom GLSL shaders, WebGL2. Python (NumPy, Rasterio, Pillow) for the terrain, trajectory and score generators. Blender Python scripts for the 3D models. FFmpeg and glTF Transform. The organ score was composed in code and rendered from CC0 pipe organ samples. 72 unit test files check the data, the timings and the credits.

Factors we considered

Accuracy: every claim on screen is traced to a primary source in an accuracy log. Honesty about what is uncertain. Protection of heritage sites. Accessibility: the whole experience works from the keyboard, with subtitles and two languages. NASA branding rules: logos and insignia were removed from every model.
